actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

supplementary_info.identification_information: Tiliqua scincoides scincoides is a highly variable subspecies, but usually displays six to nine pale bands between the nape and the hips, and often a dark prominent stripe between the eye and above the ear (Wilson and Swan 2013). T. s. intermedia is larger and the bands are often broken into variegations of accompanied by heavy mottling on the back. It is distinctly flushed with yellow or orange and has alternating black bars on the flanks (Cogger 2000, Wilson and Swan 2013).

documentation.range: Present in Australia and the Tanibar Islands of Indonesia. In Australia, Tiliqua scincoides ranges from the east of South Australia, through eastern Victoria and New South Wales to the eastern two-thirds of Queensland, and the northern coast of Northern Territory and Western Australia. T. s. scincoides occurs in the southern and eastern portions of this range, whereas T. s. intermedia occupies the north and west (Cogger 2000, Wilson and Swan 2013). There is an isolated subpopulation of T. s. scincoides in central Australia.
documentation.population: It is a common to abundant species. Tiliqua scincoides scincoides is likely stable, whereas T. s. intermedia may be experiencing population declines.
documentation.habitats: This species occupies a wide variety of habitats within its range, occurring in virtually all conditions through eastern and northern Australia, except for the alps (Wilson and Swan 2013).
documentation.threats: Cane Toads are a significant threat to this species, especially for the northern Tiliqua scincoides intermedia (Price-Rees et al. 2009). Taste aversion training may be a successful management tool to combat this threat (Price-Rees et al. 2011). In the Sydney region, despite the significant fragmentation of bush remnants, the species has persisted and is abundant throughout the suburbs, and hence, habitat loss or degradation may not pose a serious threat (Koenig et al. 2001).
documentation.measures: There are no specific conservation actions for this species. Subpopulations are present within a variety of protected areas, including 46 National Parks in Queensland (Macdonald 2012).
documentation.use_trade: This species can be kept privately with an appropriate recreational wildlife license and is used in the pet trade (Queensland Government 2017). Many individuals are captive-bred.
documentation.rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, a threat from cane toads is localized and unlikely to be resulting in rapid enough population declines to justify a threatened listing.
